q-106438:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-2x,\,{t}^{2}=-4y.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-4y$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =-4y \\ {x}^{2} & =-y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${x}^{2}=-y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =Ai=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{′} & =Aj=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i\end{aligned}
$$

q-18372:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-2\cdot 4+0\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-236734:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 4+1\cdot x+2\cdot 1 \\  & =x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32139:
This system can be written as

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}46 \\ -23\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}].$
This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-6\cdot 8}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{46}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now represent the solution to this system, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{46}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}46 \\ -23\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-114245:
If we plug in $x=1$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{[1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[{x}^{2}-2x+1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2x-2}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[2x-2]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115526:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]}^{′}}{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{-{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡0\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-88454:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3x}-25\cdot {4}^{3x} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-25)\cdot {4}^{3x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
{x}^{2}-25=0\,\text{and}\,{4}^{3x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation ${x}^{2}-25=0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+5)(x-5)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-5,5.$

- The equation ${4}^{3x}=0$ has no solutions because ${4}^{3x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-5,5,$ and their product is $(-5)\cdot 5=-25.$

q-102416:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
\sqrt[7]{3x+13}-1=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[7]{3x+13}-1 & =0 \\ \sqrt[7]{3x+13} & =1 \\ (\sqrt[7]{3x+13})^{7} & ={1}^{7} \\ 3x+13 & =1 \\ 3x & =-12 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=-4.$

q-48722:
The area of the surface area of the sphere is given by  

$$
A=A(r)=4\pi {r}^{2}
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(r)$ with respect to its radius $r$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi (2r) \\  & =8\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

q-114168:
Factoring the constant out of the integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =3(0-1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$
